D014-D008_h001.question:
It’s hard to explain without crying, honestly. For a little over two years now—about two years and a few months—I’ve just felt…low, almost all the time. I sit in that booth for eight, ten hours, and I’m exhausted before my shift even starts. It’s not just being tired from work; it’s like a heaviness in my body that doesn’t lift, even on days I sleep enough. Walking from the parking lot to the booth feels like a chore.

I find myself tearing up over the smallest things—someone snapping at me, a song on the radio, even nothing at all. I’ll turn my head so drivers don’t notice, but my eyes are almost always burning. I’ve kind of stopped expecting things to get better. After the divorce I tried to be hopeful, but now it feels like this is just how my life is going to be, no matter what I do. I still show up to work, but I’m slower, I make mistakes with change.

Every now and then I’ll have these spells where I feel unusually upbeat and talkative, work extra shifts, start planning big changes—but they fizzle out or crash into this same tired, defeated feeling, so I don’t know what to make of them.
D014-D008_h001.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder
D014-D008_h001.answer: D & C. Persistent Depressive Disorder & Bipolar I Disorder

D014-D008_h002.question:
I’ve just been feeling worn down for what feels like forever now… a little over two years, I guess. I drive the early morning subway shifts, and even on nights when I actually sleep a decent amount, I wake up exhausted, like I’ve already done a full day. It’s this heavy, dragging kind of tired that never really lifts. By the time I’m on the train, focusing on the signals takes way more effort than it used to, and when I get home, I mostly just lie on the couch. I’ve cut back on seeing friends, and I’ve stopped picking up extra shifts because I just can’t.

Sometimes I find myself tearing up over nothing, like on my break in the staff room or even on the platform when it’s quiet. It’s embarrassing, so I try to hide it. I keep thinking this is just how things are now, that it’s not going to get better no matter what I do.

Every once in a while, I’ll get these short bursts where I feel strangely wired and upbeat, like I’ve got more energy than usual and my thoughts are kind of racing ahead of me, but they don’t seem to last long or follow any pattern I can see.
D014-D008_h002.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D014-D008_h003.question:

It’s not that I’m crying all day; it’s more like everything feels muted. Even when something good happens, like landing a solo, I know I should be excited, but it barely registers. After class I’m wiped, but it’s more mental than physical. I used to daydream about future roles, touring, maybe teaching; now my mind jumps straight to what will probably go wrong. I automatically assume I’ll get injured, or be replaced, or that nothing will really change anyway.

There are these odd stretches where, for a few days, I’ll suddenly feel unusually wired—sleep less, rehearse obsessively, start planning a million projects—but it’s hard to tell if that’s just adrenaline before a performance or something else. Then I slide back into this flat, tired, negative state. It’s starting to affect my work; my director’s noticed I’m not as present or expressive on stage.

A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Persistent Depressive Disorder

D014-D008_h004.question:

D014-D008_h005.question:
I’ve just been feeling worn down for a long time now… a little over two years, I guess. I’m on a crew pouring concrete, and even on lighter days my body feels like it weighs a ton. I don’t really see things getting better. I’m 38, still renting a small place by myself, no family of my own, and I just feel like this is it—that nothing’s going to change no matter what I do.

A. Binge-Eating Disorder

D014-D008_h006.question:
I guess the main thing is that, for a little over two years now, it feels like someone turned the volume down on my emotions. Not off, just…muted. Stuff that should feel exciting—like landing a good gig or working with a big-name artist—barely registers. I go through the motions, smile when I’m supposed to, but inside it’s kind of flat.

I’m constantly comparing myself to other engineers and producers, and I always come up short in my head. Even when clients are happy, I’m thinking, “Anyone else would’ve done this better.” That’s there pretty much every day, and it makes me second-guess everything.

I get stuck on tiny decisions—what to wear to the studio, which plug‑in chain to commit to, what to order for dinner. I’ll open and close the same menu or session presets over and over because I can’t just pick something. It slows me down a lot, and I’ve missed deadlines or avoided projects because I can’t decide how to start.

Every so often, I’ll have these stretches where I suddenly feel unusually “switched on”—sleep less, talk faster, start a ton of new ideas at once in the studio—but I’m not sure if that’s just me pushing through or something else. It never seems clear where normal ends and “too much” begins.
D014-D008_h006.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Delusional Disorder
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Bipolar II Disorder

D014-D008_h007.question:

It slows me down with booking clients and finishing designs, and I’ve lost a few regulars because I drag my feet answering messages.

Every now and then I’ll get these weird stretches where my energy suddenly spikes—I sleep less, talk more, take on a bunch of tattoo projects at once, feel almost overly confident—but I can’t tell if that’s just me pushing through or something else. It never feels steady; I swing back to that low, critical place again.
D014-D008_h007.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder
    B. Delusional Disorder
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Bipolar II Disorder

Every now and then I’ll swing the other way—sleep less, talk more, take on too many projects at once—but it never seems to settle into anything clear, just adds to the feeling that something’s off.
